nodes.question: What is the observed concentration range of DEET in the aquatic environment?
nodes.answer: The observed concentration range of DEET in the aquatic environment varies from ng/L to mg/L.
nodes.paragraph: The consump - tion of DEET at large doses has also been observed to exhibit fatal toxicity. A recent study reported that there is a significant correlation between DEET and increased levels of serum uric acid in the human population and the occurrence of several chronic ailments, including gout, diabetes, hypertension, and chronic renal illnesses [9]. Conventional municipal treatment plants are not designed to handle this type of pollutant. Due to its low log Kd (dissociation constant) value of 1.91, only a mini - mum proportion of DEET can be adsorbed into waste - water sludge, soils, and landfills [10]. This results in the migration of DEET into the aquatic environment, and the detected concentration range varies from ng/L to mg/L. The early documentation of DEET detection in fresh - water environments occurred throughout the 1990s in American and European regions. Due to the significant use of DEET in personal care products (PCPs) and their application in agriculture, the presence of DEET in waste - water, surface water, and groundwater has been observed [3, 11].

nodes.label: Facts
nodes.question: What is the maximum detected concentration of DEET in the Indian aquatic matrix?
nodes.answer: The maximum detected concentration of DEET in the Indian aquatic matrix is 0.388 g/L.
nodes.paragraph: The discovered concentrations of DEET in these environmental matrices range from non-detectable levels to mg/L [12, 13]. The maximum detected concentration of DEET in the Indian aquatic matrix is 0.388 g/L [14]. Because DEET is persistent, stable, and resistant to deg - radation in water, its concentration in aquatic matrices may reach up to 1 mg/L and is expected to become much higher if left unregulated [15]. Microalgae are photosynthetic organisms that can thrive in aquatic settings and produce biomass using light for photosynthesis and carbon dioxide (CO2) as a carbon source for their growth. Microalgae S impor - tance stems from its propensity to absorb carbon dioxide (CO2), the primary greenhouse gas and cause of the global warming crisis, and convert it into bio - products [16, 17]. Microalgal technology has been reported widely for its bioremediation properties, with harvested biomass used for the production of value- added by-products that are utilized in various sectors (food, renewable energy, water purification, environ - mental management, biofertilizers, cosmetics, and medical supplies) [18, 19].

nodes.question: What are the main characteristics of Cel that hinder its clinical application?
nodes.answer: The main characteristics of Cel that hinder its clinical application are hydrophobicity, low bioavailability, and systemic toxicity.
nodes.paragraph: However, the clinical application of Cel is hindered by its unsatisfactory characteristics, including hydrophobicity, low bioavailability, and systemic toxic - ity [16]. Hence, it is necessary to develop novel delivery systems for Cel to overcome the afore-mentioned defi - ciencies in applications while optimizing immune stimulation. In this work, we constructed an injectable water-in- oil emulsion hydrogel (EHG) to load an ICD inducer- Cel in the continuous oil phase (Gel@Cel). The EHG drug delivery system was developed on the foundation of clinically established iodized oil, with the objective of enhancing its biocompatibility and facilitating its clinical translation. In addition, the EHG system was designed to demonstrate good shear-thinning viscoelastic proper - ties and a high drug-loading capacity, while overcoming the hydrophobicity of Cel. The Gel@Cel demonstrated an exceptional lipase-regulated, sustained release of Cel, which in turn triggers an ICD effect. nodes.question: What concentration of DEET requires testing due to its persistent nature?
nodes.answer: Concentrations over 2 mg/L require testing due to the persistent and stable nature of DEET.
nodes.paragraph: Concentrations over 2 mg/L require testing due to the persistent and stable nature of DEET. Chlorella vulgaris, upon stress, is known to exhibit growth-stimulating effects, which increase biochemi - cal composition accumulation that produces biomass to produce bioproducts [23]. The acute toxicity assessment has revealed that when the concentration of the DEET increases, the algal growth rate reduces to half at 96-h EC50 [24]. However, the effects of DEET on the biochemi - cal composition (proteins, lipids, and carbohydrates) and pigments (chlorophyll-A, chlorophyll-B, and carotenoids) in the acute toxicity study have not yet been investi - gated. This investigation will help us grasp the possibil - ity of assessing Chlorella vulgaris potential in treating the DEET-polluted wastewater and biochemical composition of harvested biomass for the manufacture of bioproducts from algal biomass. The primary objective of this study is to investigate the effects of DEET on the metabolic composition and pig - ment levels of Chlorella vulgaris, specifically in relation to its 96-h EC50. Additionally, the study aims to assess the influence of DEET on the removal capacity of Chlo - rella vulgaris at varying concentrations, both prior to and following the tolerance limit, as well as the associated changes in the mechanisms employed to alleviate stress in relation to this tolerance limit.
